Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (Second Circuit).

We represent: plaintiff.

Facts: Plaintiff, a journalist, was arrested while filming a protest and sues the arresting officers under 42 U.S.C. 1983 for First and Fourth Amendment violations. The officers move to dismiss on qualified immunity, asking the court to decide only whether the right was clearly established.

Assignment: Draft plaintiff's opposition argument on qualified immunity, including what framework and order of analysis the court must follow.

Research results from the firm's case-law database:

answer:
# ARGUMENT

## I. DEFENDANTS ARE NOT ENTITLED TO DISMISSAL ON QUALIFIED IMMUNITY

### A. The Governing Framework: Two Questions, Sequenced in the Court's Discretion

Qualified immunity shields officials from damages liability only where their conduct "does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known." *Harlow v. Fitzgerald*, 457 U.S. 800, 818 (1982). The inquiry has two parts: (1) whether the facts alleged make out a violation of a constitutional right, and (2) whether that right was clearly established at the time of the challenged conduct. *Pearson v. Callahan*, 555 U.S. 223, 232 (2009).

Defendants ask the Court to skip the first question and decide only the second. The Court may do so, but it is not required to. Under *Saucier v. Katz*, 533 U.S. 194, 201 (2001), courts had to resolve the constitutional question first. *Pearson* overruled that rigid sequence in relevant part and held that judges "should be permitted to exercise their sound discretion in deciding which of the two prongs . . . should be addressed first." 555 U.S. at 236. Because *Pearson* governs, the Court may begin with either prong. It may also decline to reach one, but it need not do so. *See Camreta v. Greene*, 563 U.S. 692, 705–07 (2011) (recognizing the value of deciding the constitutional question to develop the law).

Plaintiff respectfully submits that the Court should address the constitutional question first. Defendants' request would leave the right of a journalist to film police activity at a protest undefined. That is a recurring question of public importance, and deciding it first is the course that "promotes the development of constitutional precedent." *Pearson*, 555 U.S. at 236. In any event, Plaintiff prevails on both prongs.

### B. The Motion Must Be Decided on the Complaint's Allegations

Defendants move under Rule 12(b)(6). Qualified immunity can support dismissal at this stage only if the defense is established on the face of the complaint. The defense "faces a formidable hurdle," and the plaintiff is entitled to all reasonable inferences from the facts alleged. *McKenna v. Wright*, 386 F.3d 432, 436 (2d Cir. 2004). Courts must take well-pleaded facts as true and may not resolve factual disputes in the officers' favor. *See Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678–79 (2009); *Tolan v. Cotton*, 572 U.S. 650, 656–57 (2014) (per curiam). Plaintiff alleges that [he/she] was a working journalist, was filming a public protest from a public location, did not interfere with police operations, and was arrested while doing so. [Compl. ¶¶ __.] On those allegations, Defendants cannot carry their burden.

### C. The Complaint Plausibly Alleges First and Fourth Amendment Violations

*First Amendment.* Gathering news in public, including by recording police officers performing their duties in public, is protected activity. *See Glik v. Cunniffe*, 655 F.3d 78, 82–84 (1st Cir. 2011); *Fields v. City of Philadelphia*, 862 F.3d 353, 355–56 (3d Cir. 2017); *Smith v. City of Cumming*, 212 F.3d 1332, 1333 (11th Cir. 2000). Arrest in retaliation for protected speech or newsgathering violates the First Amendment. A plaintiff states such a claim by alleging protected conduct, an adverse action, and a causal connection. *See Nieves v. Bartlett*, 587 U.S. 391, 398–99 (2019). Plaintiff alleges that [he/she] was arrested because [he/she] was filming. [Compl. ¶ __.]

*Fourth Amendment.* A warrantless arrest requires probable cause. Plaintiff alleges that [he/she] committed no offense and that no reasonable officer could have believed otherwise. [Compl. ¶ __.] Whether Defendants had probable cause, or even arguable probable cause, turns on facts the Court cannot resolve against Plaintiff on this motion. *See Zalaski v. City of Hartford*, 723 F.3d 382, 389–90 (2d Cir. 2013).

Probable cause is also not a complete defense here. Under *Nieves*, the no-probable-cause requirement is relaxed where the plaintiff offers objective evidence that similarly situated people not engaged in the protected speech were not arrested. 587 U.S. at 406–07. Plaintiff will meet that standard. [Compl. ¶ __ (describing non-journalist bystanders not arrested).]

### D. The Rights at Issue Were Clearly Established

A right is clearly established when its contours are "sufficiently clear that every reasonable official would have understood that what he is doing violates that right." *Ashcroft v. al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. 731, 741 (2011) (cleaned up). That standard is met by controlling authority or "a robust consensus of cases of persuasive authority." *District of Columbia v. Wesby*, 583 U.S. 48, 63 (2018). Precedent need not involve "a case directly on point," *al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. at 741, and officials "can still be on notice that their conduct violates established law even in novel factual circumstances." *Hope v. Pelzer*, 536 U.S. 730, 741 (2002); *see also Taylor v. Riojas*, 592 U.S. 7, 8–9 (2020) (per curiam).

First, the general principle that the government may not arrest a person without probable cause, or in retaliation for protected expression, has been settled for decades. *See Nieves*, 587 U.S. at 398–99; *Zalaski*, 723 F.3d at 389–90. Second, the more specific application here also supplies fair warning. Every circuit to decide the question has recognized a First Amendment right to record police in public. *See Glik*, 655 F.3d at 82–85; *Smith*, 212 F.3d at 1333; *Fields*, 862 F.3d at 355–56; *Turner v. Lieutenant Driver*, 848 F.3d 678, 688–90 (5th Cir. 2017); *Askins v. U.S. Dep't of Homeland Sec.*, 899 F.3d 1035, 1044 (9th Cir. 2018). That consensus gave a reasonable officer fair notice, particularly where, as Plaintiff alleges, the arrestee was visibly identifiable as press and was not interfering with police activity. [Compl. ¶ __.] Whether Defendants' conduct was objectively reasonable is therefore a fact-bound question that cannot be resolved on the pleadings.

### E. Conclusion on Qualified Immunity

Under *Pearson*, the Court may take the prongs in either order. Whichever order it chooses, the complaint alleges violations of clearly established rights, and the motion to dismiss on qualified immunity should be denied. At minimum, Defendants may reassert the defense on a developed record at summary judgment.
